A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SCM/FineHarm research. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection experiments, annotation comparisons, sensitivity analyses, and SCM-assisted safety-alignment results on MT-Bench and PKU-SafeRLHF.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds baseline comparisons, latency measurements, ablations, and out-of-distribution evaluations.

M1.justification: The FineHarm annotation procedure, SCM architecture, token/holistic supervision, logical-consistency loss, Delay-k stopping, and TokenDPO objective remain unchanged. New ablations and computational discussion evaluate or explain the existing method.

E1.justification: v2 adds detection evaluation on two external distributions, ToxicChat and ToxiGen, using FineHarm-trained SCM (Appendix C.5). v1 evaluated detection on FineHarm only. FineHarm and the MT-Bench/PKU-SafeRLHF alignment tasks remain; the newly listed source LLMs document existing data provenance.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds HateBERT, ToxDectRoBERTa, Google Perspective, OpenAI Moderation, and LlamaGuard3-8B as full-detection comparators. Some services already participated in dataset annotation, but not this reported comparison. Table 5 also adds Direct labeling to the annotation-strategy comparison.

E3.justification: v2 introduces external-distribution testing after FineHarm training and a latency benchmark comparing generation and detection at three model scales, using sequence lengths from 50 to 100 without acceleration. These extend the evaluation design; the original split, accuracy metrics, threshold selection, and retained training recipes are unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds holistic-loss ablations, the Direct annotation control, an explicit beta-sensitivity study, and OOD generalization tests. The existing logic-loss ablations move unchanged from Table 2 to Table 6, and the alpha-sensitivity plot is retained. One illustrative annotation example is also replaced.

E5.justification: The new latency benchmark reports ten repetitions per test sequence and minimum, maximum, and average latency (Table 3). This introduces limited variability reporting; classification results still lack repeated-seed information or uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Original SCM macro-F1 scores of 95.64/97.91/97.45, logic-ablation scores, and alignment results are unchanged. v2 adds baseline, latency, holistic-ablation, beta-sensitivity, and OOD results, plus Direct labeling at 95.38 macro-F1. SCM-7B newly scores 70.08 on ToxicChat and 70.88 on ToxiGen; these are new evaluations, not gains on the original test.

T1.justification: Section 5.5 adds a latency model and expected-time derivation assuming uniformly distributed stopping positions and parallel generation/detection, followed by comparison with full detection (Equations 7–8). The original method's mathematical definitions and derivations remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims: FineHarm, native streaming monitoring, approximately 95%+ detection performance while observing 18% of tokens on average, and SCM-assisted safety alignment. Additional evidence does not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning OOD generalization, component contributions, saturation at larger beta values, and one-token monitoring delay when detection is sufficiently fast. The generalization statement has an exception in Table 9, where SCM-0.5B trails HateBERT. Original limitations are retained in Appendix A.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-page link, identifies nine source LLMs in the existing WildGuard data, and documents learning rates for HateBERT/ToxDectRoBERTa and the text-moderation-latest evaluation endpoint. Existing hardware, SCM training recipes, alignment settings, and annotation prompts are retained.

R1.justification: New citations cover HateBERT, ToxDectRoBERTa, ToxiGen, and speculative decoding. Appendix A adds a substantive distinction from speculative decoding through objectives, model roles, and computational savings. The main related-work section and overall research positioning remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The discussion and limitations move from main-text Section 6 to Appendix A, and experimental subsections and appendix organization expand. Header information and several headings change, but the abstract, core method exposition, related work, and conclusion are largely retained.

P2.justification: The empirical displays expand substantially: Table 2 is reorganized, ablations receive an expanded separate table, and latency/OOD tables and beta-sensitivity Figure 8 are added. Existing Figure 7 retains its alpha curves with a corrected caption. The example table also changes its selection and ordering.

improvement.justification: The external-distribution tests and established-moderator comparisons address an important weakness of v1: detection validation relied on FineHarm and a narrow comparator set. The holistic-loss ablation and latency measurements further strengthen evidence for the design and practical motivation. Although the latency argument remains conditional and the broad generalization interpretation overlooks an exception, the expanded validation substantially improves the paper's empirical foundation.
